answer:
A black hole is a region of space where so much matter is packed into such a small space that gravity stops anything from escaping, even light [1]. Its edge is the event horizon, a point of no return rather than a solid surface. Anything that crosses it can't get back out, so the region inside looks black [1][2]. Most black holes we know of form when a very massive star runs out of fuel and collapses in a supernova. These "stellar-mass" black holes start at a few times the Sun's mass. The supermassive ones at the centres of galaxies are far bigger: Sagittarius A* at the centre of our Milky Way is about 4 million Suns [1]. Black holes give off no light, so astronomers find them by their effects. Examples are hot, X-ray-bright disks of gas swirling around them, stars orbiting something unseen, gravitational waves when two black holes merge, and the way they bend light from objects behind them [1].

Sources:
[1] NASA Science, "Black Holes": https://science.nasa.gov/universe/black-holes/
[2] NASA Scientific Visualization Studio, "NASA Black Hole Visualization Takes Viewers Beyond the Brink": https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/14576
